messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I got a 22 item test and I am trying to fit a two dimensional irt model. The related syntax is:

model.priorM2 <- mirt.model('F1 = 1-22,
                             F2 = 1-22,
                             PRIOR = (1-22, d, norm, 0, 1),
                             PRIOR = (1-22, a1, lnorm, 0.5306283, 0.8143413),
                             PRIOR = (1-22, a2, lnorm, 0.5306283, 0.8143413)')

resultM2<-mirt(respcorM1,model=model.priorM2,itemtype='3PL',
                           SE=TRUE,method="EM")

However, the "discrimination" parameter estimates are the same, within each item:

$i1
             a1      a2      d     g  u
par       1.798   1.798 -0.569 0.109  1
CI_2.5  -20.083 -20.083 -1.245 0.042 NA
CI_97.5  23.680  23.680  0.107 0.253 NA

$i2
             a1      a2      d     g  u
par       1.273   1.273 -1.114 0.095  1
CI_2.5  -14.211 -14.211 -1.991 0.027 NA
CI_97.5  16.757  16.757 -0.238 0.285 NA

.
.
.

I am aware about the issues concerning the model identification of multidimensional IRT models. However, since the factors are assumed to be uncorrelated, their means and variances were set o be 0 and 1, respectively and, due to the prior choice of the "discrimination" parameters, which lead to their estimates will be always positive, the model would be already identified and no longer restrictions would be necessary (http://www.ime.unicamp.br/sites/default/files/pesquisa/relatorios/rp-2017-08.pdf).

Many thanks.

Caio

messages.subject: Re: Multidimensional IRT models
messages.body_plain:
Using a prior which restricts the range of the parameter space to be > 0 does not identify a model. You still need to impose the usual parameter constraints via the loading pattern. Think about a simple set of linear equations with 2 knowns and 3 unknowns. Knowing that the third unknown is positive still doesn't let you uniquely identify the system, it just tells you the infinite region it's associate with (not the exact point). The IRT model is the same here, so imposing lower/upper bounds or priors with bounded spaces is not sufficient for identification.

Phil

Hello mirt forum,

First, I would like to express my thanks to Dr. Chalmers for his help last week.

I'm attempting to analyze dichotomous reading comprehension data (n=10,521) for DIF with 1 reference group and 5 focal groups. I am quite new to MIRT so I apologize in advance for any obvious (or subtle) errors and would appreciate your feedback.

My understanding is that as a very first step I need to determine the dimensionality of the data. To do so I ran this code (not including multipleGroup at this stage):

mod1 <- mirt(read_mirt, 1, verbose=TRUE)
mod2 <- mirt(read_mirt, 2, verbose=TRUE)
mod3 <- mirt(read_mirt, 3, verbose=TRUE)

mirt::M2(mod1)
mirt::M2(mod2)
mirt::M2(mod3)

Here are the model fit statistics produced by M2:

> mirt::M2(mod1)
            M2  df p      RMSEA    RMSEA_5   RMSEA_95      SRMSR       TLI       CFI
stats 1522.236 405 0 0.01619336 0.01533095 0.01706289 0.01842013 0.9853581 0.9863679

> mirt::M2(mod2)
           M2  df p      RMSEA    RMSEA_5   RMSEA_95      SRMSR       TLI       CFI
stats 1035.82 376 0 0.01291549 0.01198092 0.01385578 0.01546339 0.9906858 0.9919491

> mirt::M2(mod3)
            M2  df p      RMSEA     RMSEA_5 RMSEA_95      SRMSR       TLI       CFI
stats 784.1172 348 0 0.01091451 0.009897989 0.011932 0.01353918 0.9933483 0.9946786

I've read that SRMSR less than .05 is acceptable, and that TLI and CFI greater than .95 are acceptable. (I've also heard that RMSEA itself is not ideal for model selection.) However, I'm unsure if these are cut-offs, or if relatively smaller SRMSR and greater TLI/CFI are considered better fits (along the lines of BIC/AIC interpretations).  Therefore, I am not sure which of these models is a better fit.

Although I am not entirely sure this is how I should proceed, I calculated AIC and BIC using the anova method. This appears to show that 2 or 3 dimensions are preferable to 1. Comparing 2 to 3 dimensions, 3 dimensions appears preferable for all indices except non-sample size adjusted BIC.

> anova (mod1, mod2)

Model 1: mirt(data = read_mirt, model = 1, verbose = TRUE)

       AIC     AICc    SABIC      BIC    logLik      X2  df   p
1 268046.1 268046.8 268291.1 268481.8 -133963.1     NaN NaN NaN
2 267554.0 267556.6 268031.7 268403.5 -133660.0 606.143  57   0

> anova (mod2, mod3)

Model 1: mirt(data = read_mirt, model = 2, verbose = TRUE)
Model 2: mirt(data = read_mirt, model = 3, verbose = TRUE)

       AIC     AICc    SABIC      BIC    logLik      X2  df   p
1 267718.3 267719.9 268081.7 268364.6 -133770.2     NaN NaN NaN
2 267554.0 267556.6 268031.7 268403.5 -133660.0 220.335  28   0

It appears the best-fitting IRT model has three dimensions. If the forum could provide advice about model fit, I would appreciate it very much.

(Note: is it necessary to run 4-dimensional model for comparison?)

Thank you!
Jeanne

Probably not. That said, the test structure seems to be fairly well fit by even a uni-dimensional model according to the fit statistics. You may do just as well using that model and avoiding multidimensionality all together. Whether that's valid or not is up to your theoretical structure (the reasons you're seeing such differences in anova() is largely a function of your sample size). Higher-dimensional models will almost always fit the data better because they use considerably more parameters.

For DIF testing though, you really should establish the pattern of loadings first (think exploratory factor analysis to get to confirmatory factor analysis). Otherwise, you'll be performing DIF analyses that are largely meaningless. Check out the loadings pattern via summary() and see if it makes sense theoretically for these models.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

I think that I understood your point but I see no relation with this issue of identifiability. I, kindly, disagree with you. In the paper that I have mentioned we have discussed some issues concerning the identification of mirt models (there are other details in another paper not finished yet and the Master's Thesis of my student, written in Portuguese). In all simulation studies that her performed,under these restrictions, the parameters were well recovered. When we fix the latent trait mean vector in zero and the covariance matrix as the identidity, only ortoghonal transformations are allowed in the linear latent predictor (a*theta). Therefore, due to the nature of the ortoghonal matrices (say T), any transformation as (a*T’*T*theta) will lead, always, to an a*=a*T’, with a different sign of “a” (provided that its components have the same sign), which is not allowed since we are restricting "a" to be positives. I am currently doing some other simulations and we can provide the related results.

Best,

Caio

> Using a prior which restricts the range of the parameter space to be > 0 does not identify a model. You still need to impose the usual parameter constraints via the loading pattern. Think about a simple set of linear equations with 2 knowns and 3 unknowns. Knowing that the third unknown is positive still doesn't let you uniquely identify the system, it just tells you the infinite region it's associate with (not the exact point). The IRT model is the same here, so imposing lower/upper bounds or priors with bounded spaces is not sufficient for identification.

messages.subject: Re: What's the item remove standard based on h2?

In many cases, the rule of thumb of item selection have followed the tradition of structural equation modelling, that is not fit well with MIRT theories.

The basic of item selection rule may be present three parts: check model SE reached local maximum, check item fit and combinate items using item information (xxIRT package may help you). But that is not always "standard", so that You may have to learn IRT basics and psychometric theories.

Moreover, statistical indices are not crucial than item quality like readability, differential item functioning by SES (Social-Economic Status), Adverse Impact for disability, etc. Statistical indices just help you can find out the test can be fair. HTH.

Seongho

messages.subject: Re: model identification
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeanne,

This model looks identified, but I'm not sure where you're trying to
go with this DIF analysis. It seems as though you want to test bias in
each multidimensional item, however you're uncertain of the loading
structure (hence, the use of CONSTRAIN and exploratory IRT models).
DIF testing is a fairly advanced topic in the measurement modelling
process, which occurs only after a suitable loading pattern has been
established (note that unidimensional IRT models don't have this
problem because the confirmatory pattern is automatically identified
in a restrictive way due to requiring all items to load on one
construct). So, it looks here like you're investigating DIF for and
exploratory IRT model....which feels a little on the peculiar side.

My observation last time about non-identifiability was because you
freed that latent mean and variance parameters for both groups instead
of just the focal group(s). Here it looks like your model is setup
better, though you could actually remove all the CONSTRAIN arguments
and it still would be identified (the anchor item constraints, via
CONSTAINB, are automatically being applied through the "invariance"
argument). HTH.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: test IRT assumptions for rasch model with missing data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am currently working on a project in which I tested 1677 participants on a subset of >1700 items.
Due to the design, a big majority of the data is missing values. That is because every participant could only be tested on a limited amount of items, and every item could appear in two versions both at test and presentation (which adds the variables "item_version" and "old/new"). In the end, separating all these conditions, only roughly 2,6 % of items were answered by each participant.

Using a unidimensional Rasch model, my goal is to select those items that differentiate well between bad and good participants. A second goal is to get good and reliable ability estimates for the participants.

1) I therefore first want to test whether the assumptions for using a Rasch model are met.
    a)Testing for differential item functioning, I found the wald-function, but it only returns a vector of num-char pairs. Is there a way to get the chi-squared and associated p-value?

    b)Also I would like to test the assumption of local stochastic independence. Is there a function to do this in the mirt-package?

2) Given this great amount of missing data, would you advise imputing missing data, or is there another sensible way of testing model fit?

3) Finally, I would be interested in testing for potential multi-dimensionality. For instance, I was wondering whether "old/new" could be seen as two dimensions of one item and put into one model. Would this be feasible with mirt?

I hope those are not too many questions at once and thank you a lot in advance for any advise!

The Wald test is actually a X^2 test asymptotically, but I assume you are looking for the likelihood ratio test. Yes, just fit two models via multipleGroup(), where one model is the nested version of the other, and pass both to the anova() generic.

>
>     b)Also I would like to test the assumption of local stochastic independence. Is there a function to do this in the mirt-package?

Given that much missingness you're going to be limited to the point-wise estimate statistics; namely, the Q3 stat. See method?residuals('SingleGroupClass') for the helpfile related to the residuals() function.

>
> 2) Given this great amount of missing data, would you advise imputing missing data, or is there another sensible way of testing model fit?

With that much missingness no, you have to resort to full-information statistics or methods that essentially dodge the problem (like secondary point estimates can). Global fit will likely be an issue, but you could still have some luck with detecting itemmisfit via itemfit().

>
> 3) Finally, I would be interested in testing for potential multi-dimensionality. For instance, I was wondering whether "old/new" could be seen as two dimensions of one item and put into one model. Would this be feasible with mirt?

Yes, see the mirt.model() function definitions to define your loadings pattern.

Phil
